title: 13th sitting of the 20th Majlis
summary: The sitting opened at 09:01 with 55 members present, none on leave and 3 on official travel. An urgent motion from the Kendhoo member about political appointments and dismissals at state-owned companies was voted down 12 to 57, so it was not debated. A Sri Lanka criminal legal-assistance treaty was sent to the Foreign Relations Committee, and members then debated, at first reading, a bill letting private colleges become universities more easily. Debate on that bill ended with the vote on accepting it left for the voting time, and debate on a Penal Code amendment bill had just begun when this part ends. This part opens partway through the debate on the government's bill to add a cybercrime chapter to the Penal Code, and eight more members spoke before the sponsor, Hussain Riza Adam, replied. Speakers backed the bill and several asked the committee to consult technical experts and tighten how evidence is gathered. After a recess the Majlis voted three bills through to committee: higher education amendment (82-0), Penal Code cybercrime amendment (81-0) and copyright amendment (82-0). The Speaker said there would be no sitting on 10 July because of a two-day induction programme, and the next sitting is 15 July 2024. The opening speaker's header is in part 1, so that turn is not counted here.

speakers.name: Mauroof Zakir
positions: Urgent motion: called on government to stop adding staff to state companies and dismissing existing employees, and to reinstate those dismissed.
On the higher education bill: supports it, wants fixed conditions in law, quality checks and committee consultation.

speakers.name: Hassan Zareer
positions: Supports the bill but says the education system also needs review, including graduate readiness and work culture.
Welcomed the amendments but asked for fixes to the intent wording and to evidence-gathering procedures so offenders are not freed on technicalities.

speakers.name: Hussain Riza Adam
positions: Took the floor to open the debate on the Penal Code amendment bill; his speech continues in the next part.
As sponsor, said the debate showed the bill's importance; welcomed further committee work with experts and expected it to reduce cybercrime.

speakers.name: Abdulla Rifau
positions: Presented the bill: colleges registered for 15 years could convert to universities if they meet set conditions on programmes, students, staff and facilities.

speakers.name: Meekail Ahmed Nasym
positions: Said the bill was rushed and appeared to serve business interests, and questioned the government's handling of higher education and appointments.

speakers.name: Munthazim Ibrahim
positions: Supports the bill, citing a role for private colleges, and urged committee consultation with all colleges.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Shujau
positions: Supports the bill, arguing a stronger private sector and private-college universities would improve access to higher education.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Naseem
positions: Supports the bill, arguing private universities could attract foreign students and expand educational tourism.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Said the bill mainly changes who sets the conditions and the college name and location rules, and criticised the earlier government's record on education.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Didi
positions: Supports the bill and the 15-year limit, saying private universities help the economy and criticising opposition remarks.

speakers.name: Mohamed Afoo Hamid
positions: Supports the bill, noting degree allowances owed to teachers, and stressed quality and fixed conditions in law.

speakers.name: Saudulla Hilmy
positions: Supports the bill, saying more universities keep money and students in the country, and defended college founders.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ibrahim
positions: Supports the main proposals; says learning has no age limit and quality safeguards should be set in committee.

speakers.name: Hussain Hameed
positions: Supports the bill, asking for reviewed course quality and for universities to have campuses across the atolls.

speakers.name: Mohamed Musthafa Ibrahim
positions: Supports the bill, arguing for a minimum share of PhD-holding and permanent academic staff at new universities.

speakers.name: Ahmed Riyaz
positions: Called the bill a good government initiative with tighter conditions than now, and urged its quick passage.

speakers.name: Mohamed Abbas
positions: Supports the bill, saying it opens university access, keeps money in the country, and urging fee levels set with affordability in mind.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Supports the bill, arguing the private sector must be strengthened and the committee should consult those affected.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ali
positions: Supports the bill; suggests the 15-year rule and the 1,000-student requirement be reconsidered and that colleges need proper campuses.

speakers.name: Abdul Sattar Mohamed
positions: Backed the bill as timely; said cybercrime harms individuals, businesses and government, and that making identity theft, fraud and data breaches offences should help cut them.

speakers.name: Husnee Mubarik
positions: Said offences such as cyberstalking are not defined, which blocks prosecution; asked the committee to study the bill further so it becomes law quickly.

speakers.name: Ahmed Aifan
positions: Supported the bill; said the lack of specific cybercrime provisions makes courts struggle to punish offenders and that the amendments will ease this.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ismail
positions: Said earlier amendments did not cover cybercrime; expected the bill to help police and judges and to reduce such crimes.

speakers.name: Ismail Nizar
positions: Called the bill very important; said firm penalties will deter offenders and that experts should be consulted in committee.

speakers.name: Ameen Faisal
positions: Supported the bill; asked the committee to consult technology experts and foreign practice so the law stays workable as technology changes.

speakers.name: Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir
positions: Supported the bill and its definitions; argued that freedom ends where another person's begins; said the committee should hear specialists before finalising.

decisions: The urgent motion on political appointments and dismissals at state companies was not accepted for debate (12 for, 57 against).
The Sri Lanka mutual legal assistance treaty was referred to the Foreign Relations Committee.
Debate on the higher education amendment bill (2021/7) concluded; the vote on accepting it was left for the voting time.
Committee deadlines announced: 25 July 2024 (Social Committee) and 31 July 2024 (Finance Committee, two bills).
Higher Education and Training law amendment bill accepted for study and sent to the National Development and Heritage Committee.
Penal Code (Law 9/2014) cybercrime amendment bill accepted for study and sent to the Judiciary Committee.
Copyright and Related Rights Act (Law 23/2010) amendment bill accepted for study and sent to the Economic Committee.
A motion by Mauroof Zakir (Kendhoo) to debate an urgent matter, recorded in the voting appendix at 9:14 AM, did not pass.
No Majlis sitting on 10 July 2024 (induction programme for members, 10-11 July); next sitting Monday 15 July 2024 at 9:00.
